draft.title: Formal spoken presentations
card: A formal presentation starts by greeting the audience and stating the topic. It may also say what the speaker will cover, so listeners know what to expect.
The body has a clear order. Each point gets its own part, with a reason or an example, and the speaker uses words such as first, next and finally to show where they are.
The end sums up the main points and finishes on a clear final message. It does not add new points.
The speaker picks words to suit the audience, such as a class, a principal or a visiting panel. Formal speech uses full sentences and avoids slang and very casual phrases.
draft.remember: A formal presentation has a clear start, an ordered middle, a firm end and words that suit the audience.

a.q: Which sentence would best open a formal presentation to a school assembly about recycling?
opts: Good morning, everyone. Today I will explain recycling
Hey guys, so, recycling, yeah, it's kind of a big deal
Recycling is good, and that is all I really want to say
In conclusion, recycling saves resources and our school
a.why: The first option greets the audience, states the topic and uses formal words. The last option is tempting because it is well written, but a conclusion belongs at the end, not the start.
a.clue: An opening greets the audience and names the topic.

b.q: Priya is giving a talk to her Year 7 class on why sleep matters. She has finished her three points. What should her last part do?
opts: Sum up her three points and end on a clear final message
Add a fourth point about sleep that she forgot to mention
Switch to casual slang so the talk ends in a relaxed way
Repeat her greeting and topic again to start the talk over
b.why: A conclusion sums up the main points and ends on a clear message. Adding a new point is tempting, but the card says a conclusion does not add new points, so it would leave the talk unfinished.
b.clue: The ending pulls together what the audience has already heard.
